ABSTRACT Hypoxemia is readily detectable by assessing SpO 2 levels, and these are important in optimizing COVID-19 patient management. Hyperlactatemia is a marker of tissue hypoxia, particularly in patients with increased oxygen requirement and microvascular obstruction. We monitored peripheral venous lactate concentrations in hospitalized patients with moderate to severe COVID-19 ( n = 18) and in mild ambulatory COVID-19 patients in home quarantine ( n = 16). Whole blood lactate decreased significantly during the clinical course and recovery in hospitalized patients ( P = 0.008). The blood lactate levels were significantly higher in hospitalized patients than ambulatory patients (day 1: hospitalized versus ambulatory patients P = 0.002; day 28: hospitalized versus ambulatory patients P = < 0.0001). Elevated lactate levels may be helpful in risk stratification, and serial monitoring of lactate may prove useful in the care of hospitalized COVID-19 patients. Severe SARS-CoV-2 causes pneumonia and hypoxemia, often out of proportion to symptoms reported by COVID-19 patients. 1 Hypoxemia is readily detectable by assessing SpO 2 levels, and these are important in optimizing patient management. The degree to which systemic hypoxemia results in tissue hypoxemia and an increase in anaerobic glycolysis is unknown in COVID-19. Several factors could mitigate the tissue effects of decreased oxygen diffusion capacity in the lungs, including increased oxygen delivery by a right shift in the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve (Bohr effect), increased fractional unloading of oxygen, and increased hemoglobin concentrations. Hyperlactatemia is one marker of tissue hypoxia, particularly when anaerobic tissue metabolism is increased in infections where there is anemia, fever with increased oxygen requirement, and microvascular obstruction. Severe malaria exemplifies these predispositions, and increased lactate levels (≥ 5 mmol/L), particularly if they are sustained after admission, are one of the best prognostic indicators of disease severity and fatal outcomes. 2 Lactate levels are also associated with poor clinical outcomes, as observed in a recent retrospective observational study in patients with COVID-19 pneumonia. 3

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated peripheral venous lactate concentrations in hospitalized patients with moderate to severe COVID-19 and mild ambulatory COVID-19 patients, comparing these levels to non-SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia and malaria cases. Findings indicate that lactate levels are significantly higher in hospitalized COVID-19 patients, decrease during recovery, and remain elevated in a subgroup with prolonged viral positivity, suggesting lactate's utility in risk stratification and monitoring disease severity and course.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational Monitoring of COVID-19 Disease Progression
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study comparing peripheral venous lactate concentrations in two groups: 18 hospitalized patients with moderate to severe COVID-19 and 16 ambulatory patients with mild COVID-19. Lactate levels were monitored longitudinally on days 1, 7, 14, and 28 for hospitalized patients, and days 1, 14, and 28 for ambulatory patients. No therapeutic intervention or dose comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Median whole blood lactate levels were 3.3 mmol/L in hospitalized COVID-19 patients and 1.4 mmol/L in ambulatory patients on day 1 (P = 0.002).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of anaerobic metabolism and cellular stress, often associated with tissue hypoxia or increased metabolic demand.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Comparison between hospitalized moderate to severe COVID-19 patients and mild ambulatory COVID-19 patients at disease onset.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates more severe disease in hospitalized COVID-19 patients at disease onset, useful for risk stratification.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Median whole blood lactate levels were 1.9 mmol/L in hospitalized patients and 1.5 mmol/L in ambulatory patients on day 28 (P < 0.0001).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of anaerobic metabolism and cellular stress, often associated with tissue hypoxia or increased metabolic demand.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Comparison between hospitalized moderate to severe COVID-19 patients and mild ambulatory COVID-19 patients at later stages of recovery.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates persistent metabolic differences between hospitalized and ambulatory COVID-19 patients even at later stages of recovery.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Median whole blood lactate levels in hospitalized patients decreased significantly from 3.3 mmol/L (day 1) to 1.9 mmol/L (day 28) during clinical course and recovery (P = 0.008).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of anaerobic metabolism and cellular stress, often associated with tissue hypoxia or increased metabolic demand.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Clinical course and recovery in hospitalized moderate to severe COVID-19 patients.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates improvement in clinical condition and recovery from COVID-19; useful for monitoring disease progression.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Consistently elevated in four hospitalized patients with prolonged SARS-CoV-2 viral positivity on day 7.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of anaerobic metabolism and cellular stress, often associated with tissue hypoxia or increased metabolic demand.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Hospitalized COVID-19 patients with prolonged SARS-CoV-2 viral positivity (beyond day 7).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Associated with delayed viral clearance and potentially more persistent disease activity or metabolic dysfunction in hospitalized COVID-19 patients.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Moderately elevated compared to non-SARS-CoV-2 infections; median level of around 4 mmol/L for severe COVID-19 (CURB-65 ">= 4"); levels > 5 mmol/L associated with severe disease and fatal outcomes in malaria.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of anaerobic metabolism and tissue hypoxia, reflecting processes like decreased oxygen diffusion in lungs (COVID-19 pneumonia) or microvascular obstruction (malaria).
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Hospitalized patients with severe COVID-19 pneumonia (CURB-65 >= 4) and comparison to severe systemic infections like malaria.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates severe disease, predicts fatal outcomes (especially in severe systemic infections), and reflects a longer course of illness in COVID-19. Useful for general risk stratification and understanding distinct pathophysiological processes.
